topic: Complex, high-performance and technically advanced airplanes

notes.front: What is a controllable-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A propeller whose blade angle can be changed in flight, instead of being fixed.
notes.explanation: Making the blade angle controllable is what improves propeller efficiency across a wide range of operation.
notes.example: Like a bicycle with gears rather than a single fixed gear: the blade angle can be changed to suit the speed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Controllable-Pitch Propeller"
notes.evidence: To provide improved propeller efficiency through a wide range of operation, the propeller blade angle needs to be controllable.

notes.front: What is a complex airplane?
notes.back: An airplane with retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller (or a digital engine control system in place of the propeller control).
notes.explanation: For a landplane all three are needed; a seaplane counts as complex with flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller alone.
notes.example: Like a fixed-gear trainer, but with wheels that fold away and a propeller whose pitch the pilot sets.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: Complex airplane means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller, including airplanes equipped with an engine control system consisting of a digital computer and associated accessories for controlling the engine and propeller
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a high-performance airplane?
notes.back: An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower.
notes.explanation: The definition rests on engine power alone, not on gear, flaps or propeller.
notes.example: Like a family car with a big engine: a single-engine six-seater with a 300-horsepower engine is one.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (f)(1)
notes.evidence: a high-performance airplane (an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a propeller's governing range?
notes.back: The range of blade angles between the high and low pitch stops.
notes.explanation: Inside that range the governor can hold the selected rpm; at a stop it cannot.
notes.example: Like a car's cruise control, which holds the speed only until the throttle is fully open or fully closed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Governing Range"
notes.evidence: The range of possible blade angles between high and low blade angle pitch stops define the propeller's governing range.

notes.front: What is the critical altitude of a turbocharged airplane?
notes.back: The altitude, specified by the manufacturer, up to which the turbocharger maintains maximum allowable sea-level manifold pressure.
notes.explanation: The term belongs to altitude turbocharging, which holds sea-level manifold pressure up to that altitude.
notes.example: Like a pump that keeps a hose at full pressure up to a certain height, above which the pressure falls away.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: maintains maximum allowable sea level manifold pressure (normally 29–30 "Hg) up to a certain altitude. This altitude is specified by the airplane manufacturer and is referred to as the airplane's critical altitude.

notes.front: What is a turbocharger's waste gate?
notes.back: A bypass that diverts some exhaust overboard before it passes through the turbine.
notes.explanation: The turbine can produce more manifold pressure than the engine allows, so some exhaust is routed around it.
notes.example: Like a spillway beside a water wheel, letting part of the flow go round it instead of through it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: In order not to exceed the maximum allowable manifold pressure, a bypass or waste gate is used so that some of the exhaust is diverted overboard before it passes through the turbine.

notes.front: What is the pressure controller in a turbocharger system?
notes.back: The control centre of the system: it senses compressor discharge needs and controls oil pressure to the waste gate actuator.
notes.explanation: It reduces turbocharging to one control, the throttle.
notes.example: Like a thermostat that opens and closes a valve so the occupant only sets the dial.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: The control center of the turbocharger system is the pressure controller. This device simplifies turbocharging to one control: the throttle.

notes.front: What is an over-boost condition?
notes.back: An excessive rise in manifold pressure during normal advancement of the throttle, possibly from faulty operation of the waste gate.
notes.explanation: The handbook treats it as a turbocharger failure, with its own procedure.
notes.example: Like a pressure cooker climbing past its safe pressure because its valve has stuck.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Over-Boost Condition"
notes.evidence: If an excessive rise in manifold pressure occurs during normal advancement of the throttle (possibly owing to faulty operation of the waste gate):

notes.front: What is a squat switch?
notes.back: A landing gear safety switch, usually mounted on a main gear shock strut.
notes.explanation: It senses the airplane's weight on the gear through the compressed strut.
notes.example: Like a lift door switch that stops the car moving while the door is open.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: A landing gear safety switch, sometimes referred to as a squat switch, is usually mounted in a bracket on one of the main gear shock struts.

notes.front: A complex airplane includes one with an engine control system of a digital computer and accessories, such as a {{c1::full authority digital engine control}}.
notes.explanation: Such a system controls the engine and propeller, and the definition counts it with the controllable-pitch propeller.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: including airplanes equipped with an engine control system consisting of a digital computer and associated accessories for controlling the engine and propeller, such as a full authority digital engine control
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the pilot control engine rpm in an airplane with a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: Indirectly, with the propeller control, which is connected to the propeller governor.
notes.explanation: The governor then keeps the blade angle adjusted for maximum efficiency in most flight conditions.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller"
notes.evidence: The pilot controls the engine rpm indirectly by means of a propeller control, which is connected to the propeller governor.

notes.front: What happens when the pilot pulls the propeller control back?
notes.back: The blades move to a higher pitch; the extra load slows the engine until the forces reach equilibrium.
notes.explanation: Higher pitch raises the air resistance on the spinning propeller, which is the load that slows the engine.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller"
notes.evidence: pulling back on the propeller control moves the propeller blades to a higher pitch. This increases the air resistance exerted on the spinning propeller and puts an additional load on the engine, which causes it to slow down until the forces reach equilibrium.

notes.front: What happens to engine rpm once the propeller blades reach a pitch stop?
notes.back: It rises or falls with changes in airspeed and propeller load, as with a fixed-pitch propeller.
notes.explanation: At a stop the blades can turn no further, so the governor can no longer hold the selected rpm.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Governing Range"
notes.evidence: once the propeller blades reach their pitch-stop limit, the engine rpm increases or decreases with changes in airspeed and propeller load similar to a fixed-pitch propeller.

notes.front: With a constant-speed propeller, in what order are the controls moved when increasing power?
notes.back: Increase the rpm first, then the manifold pressure.
notes.explanation: The sequence avoids the combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: A combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm can induce damaging detonation. In order to avoid these situations, the following sequence should be followed when making power changes. ⦁ When increasing power, increase the rpm first and then the manifold pressure

notes.front: With a constant-speed propeller, in what order are the controls moved when decreasing power?
notes.back: Decrease the manifold pressure first, then the rpm.
notes.explanation: It is the reverse of the increasing sequence, and for the same purpose of avoiding high manifold pressure with low rpm.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: When decreasing power, decrease the manifold pressure first and then decrease the rpm

notes.front: What can a combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm induce?
notes.back: Damaging detonation.
notes.explanation: Excessive manifold pressure also raises cylinder combustion pressures and engine temperatures.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: Excessive manifold pressure raises the cylinder combustion pressures, resulting in high stresses within the engine. Excessive pressure also produces high-engine temperatures. A combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm can induce damaging detonation.

notes.front: Where do the exhaust gases go when the waste gate is closed?
notes.back: All of them pass through and drive the turbine.
notes.explanation: Opening the waste gate routes some exhaust around the turbine, so its position regulates the turbine's output.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: The position of the waste gate regulates the output of the turbine and therefore, the compressed air available to the engine. When the waste gate is closed, all of the exhaust gases pass through and drive the turbine.

notes.front: Once the desired manifold pressure is set in a system with a pressure controller, how much throttle adjustment is needed as altitude changes?
notes.back: Virtually none.
notes.explanation: The controller adjusts the waste gate to hold the manifold pressure called for by the throttle.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Once the desired manifold pressure is set, virtually no throttle adjustment is required with changes in altitude.

notes.front: What does altitude turbocharging, sometimes called "normalizing", do?
notes.back: It maintains maximum allowable sea-level manifold pressure, normally 29–30 inches of mercury, up to a certain altitude.
notes.explanation: That altitude is the critical altitude, specified by the manufacturer.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Altitude turbocharging (sometimes called “normalizing”) is accomplished by using a turbocharger that maintains maximum allowable sea level manifold pressure (normally 29–30 "Hg) up to a certain altitude.

notes.front: What is ground boosting?
notes.back: Turbocharging in which more than the standard 29 inches of manifold pressure is used in flight.
notes.explanation: In some ground-boosted airplanes, takeoff manifold pressure may reach 45 inches of mercury.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Ground boosting, on the other hand, is an application of turbocharging where more than the standard 29 inches of manifold pressure is used in flight. In various airplanes using ground boosting, takeoff manifold pressures may go as high as 45 "Hg.

notes.front: What happens to manifold pressure above the critical altitude?
notes.back: It decreases as additional altitude is gained.
notes.explanation: Beyond the critical altitude the turbocharger can no longer hold sea-level manifold pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Above the critical altitude, the manifold pressure decreases as additional altitude is gained.

notes.front: Which two temperatures are especially important in operating a turbocharged engine?
notes.back: Turbine inlet temperature (or exhaust gas temperature) and cylinder head temperature.
notes.explanation: The first limit protects the turbocharger's hot section; the second protects the engine's internal parts.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Heat Management"
notes.evidence: There are two temperatures that are especially important—turbine inlet temperature (TIT) or, in some installations, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and cylinder head temperature. TIT or EGT limits are set to protect the elements in the hot section of the turbocharger, while cylinder head temperature limits protect the engine's internal parts.

notes.front: What should the pilot do first in an over-boost condition?
notes.back: Immediately retard the throttle smoothly, to keep manifold pressure below the maximum for the rpm and mixture setting.
notes.explanation: The pilot then operates the engine so as to avoid a further over-boost.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Over-Boost Condition"
notes.evidence: Immediately retard the throttle smoothly to limit the manifold pressure below the maximum for the rpm and mixture setting. ⦁ Operate the engine in such a manner as to avoid a further over-boost condition.

notes.front: What may low manifold pressure in a turbocharged engine indicate, and what does the handbook advise?
notes.back: Possibly a serious exhaust leak; shut the engine down by the engine failure procedures unless a greater emergency warrants running it.
notes.explanation: If the engine is kept running, the handbook advises the lowest power the situation demands and landing as soon as practicable.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Low Manifold Pressure"
notes.evidence: it is quite possible that a serious exhaust leak has occurred creating a potentially hazardous situation: ⦁ Shut down the engine in accordance with the recommended engine failure procedures, unless a greater emergency exists that warrants continued engine operation.

notes.front: What powers an electrical landing gear retraction system?
notes.back: An electrically driven motor; the system is basically an electrically driven jack for raising and lowering the gear.
notes.explanation: Once started, the motor runs until an up or down limit switch on its gearbox is tripped.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Systems"
notes.evidence: An electrical landing gear retraction system utilizes an electrically-driven motor for gear operation. The system is basically an electrically-driven jack for raising and lowering the gear.

notes.front: What moves the gear in a hydraulic landing gear retraction system?
notes.back: Pressurised hydraulic fluid acting on linkages, from an engine-driven or electrically powered pump.
notes.explanation: With an electrically powered pump the system is called electrohydraulic.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Systems"
notes.evidence: A hydraulic landing gear retraction system utilizes pressurized hydraulic fluid to actuate linkages to raise and lower the gear.

notes.front: When does a landing gear warning horn sound?
notes.back: When the airplane is configured for landing and the landing gear is not down and locked.
notes.explanation: The horn is normally linked to throttle or flap position and/or the airspeed indicator.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: Most airplanes with a retractable landing gear have a gear warning horn that sounds when the airplane is configured for landing and the landing gear is not down and locked.

notes.front: Which device preventing accidental gear retraction is built into the retraction system and operated automatically by it?
notes.back: Mechanical downlocks.
notes.explanation: They are one of three kinds of device the handbook lists, with safety switches and ground locks.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: Mechanical downlocks are built-in components of a gear retraction system and are operated automatically by the gear retraction system.

notes.front: Which devices are installed to prevent accidental operation of the downlocks and inadvertent retraction while the airplane is on the ground?
notes.back: Electrically operated safety switches.
notes.explanation: The squat switch on a main gear strut is one such switch.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: To prevent accidental operation of the downlocks and inadvertent landing gear retraction while the airplane is on the ground, electrically-operated safety switches are installed.

notes.front: What are ground locks, and how is it shown whether they are installed?
notes.back: Removable devices, such as pins or clips, that prevent gear collapse on the ground; they usually carry red streamers.
notes.explanation: The streamers make it plain at a glance whether the locks are still installed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: All types of ground locks usually have red streamers permanently attached to them to readily indicate whether or not they are installed.

notes.front: What does a squat switch do while the strut is compressed by the airplane's weight?
notes.back: It opens the electrical circuit to the motor or mechanism that powers retraction.
notes.explanation: Once the weight is off the gear, as on takeoff, the switch releases and the gear can retract.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: When the strut is compressed by the weight of the airplane, the switch opens the electrical circuit to the motor or mechanism that powers retraction.

notes.front: In airplanes with an emergency gear release handle, what does operating it do?
notes.back: It releases the uplocks so the gear can free fall or extend under its own weight.
notes.explanation: The handle is linked mechanically to the uplocks, so it works when the main power system has failed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Emergency Gear Extension Systems"
notes.evidence: The emergency gear extension system lowers the landing gear if the main power system fails. Some airplanes have an emergency release handle in the flight deck, which is connected through a mechanical linkage to the gear uplocks. When the handle is operated, it releases the uplocks and allows the gear to free fall or extend under their own weight.

notes.front: On a go-around with flaps extended, why does the pitch-up tendency not disappear as the flaps retract?
notes.back: Because of the trim setting used to offset the nose-down pitching moment of the flaps.
notes.explanation: Full power adds airflow over the wing and tail, so the pilot should be ready for rapid changes in pitch forces.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Operational Procedures"
notes.evidence: The pitch-up tendency does not diminish completely with flap retraction because of the trim setting.

notes.front: How does the Airplane Flying Handbook say transition to a complex or high-performance airplane should be done?
notes.back: Through a structured course of training by a competent and qualified flight instructor, following a ground and flight syllabus.
notes.explanation: The goal is to reach the proficiency standards of the Airman Certification Standards for the pilot's certificate.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Transition Training"
notes.evidence: Transition to a complex airplane or a high-performance airplane should be accomplished through a structured course of training administered by a competent and qualified flight instructor. The training should be accomplished in accordance with a ground and flight training syllabus.

notes.front: An airplane has retractable gear, flaps, a constant-speed propeller and a 200-horsepower engine. How is it classed?
notes.back: A) Complex but not high-performance
notes.choices:
A) Complex but not high-performance
B) Complex and high-performance
C) High-performance but not complex
D) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: high-performance needs more than 200 horsepower, and 200 is not more. D: it has all three complex features.
notes.explanation: It meets the complex definition, but the engine does not exceed 200 horsepower.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (f)(1)
notes.evidence: a high-performance airplane (an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A landplane has fixed gear, flaps, a constant-speed propeller and a 260-horsepower engine. How is it classed?
notes.back: C) High-performance only
notes.choices:
A) Complex and high-performance
B) Complex only
C) High-performance only
D) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: without retractable gear it is not complex. D: 260 horsepower is more than 200.
notes.explanation: The engine alone decides high-performance, and the fixed gear rules out complex.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: Complex airplane means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In level cruise a pilot eases the propeller control back and leaves the throttle alone. What happens?
notes.back: D) The blades go to higher pitch and rpm falls
notes.choices:
A) The blades go to lower pitch and rpm rises
B) Nothing: the governor ignores the control
C) Manifold pressure falls to zero
D) The blades go to higher pitch and rpm falls
notes.choicesExplained: A describes advancing the control. C: the throttle, not the propeller control, sets manifold pressure. B: the control changes the governor's setting.
notes.explanation: Pulling the control back increases blade pitch and the load on the engine, so rpm settles lower.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller"
notes.evidence: pulling back on the propeller control moves the propeller blades to a higher pitch. This increases the air resistance exerted on the spinning propeller and puts an additional load on the engine, which causes it to slow down until the forces reach equilibrium.

notes.front: In a steep, fast descent the rpm creeps above the selected value although the propeller control has not moved. What is the likeliest reason?
notes.back: A) The blades have reached the high pitch stop
notes.choices:
A) The blades have reached the high pitch stop
B) The governor has increased blade angle too far
C) The waste gate has stuck closed
D) The blades have reached the low pitch stop
notes.choicesExplained: B: at the stop the blade angle can increase no further. C: a waste gate affects manifold pressure, not governing. D: the low stop is reached as airspeed falls.
notes.explanation: As airspeed rises the blades increase pitch until the high stop; after that rpm rises with airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Governing Range"
notes.evidence: Conversely, if the airspeed increases, the pitch angle of the propeller blades increase until the high pitch stop is reached. The engine rpm then begins to increase.

notes.front: Flying a constant-speed propeller at reduced power, the pilot needs more power. Which is the correct first action?
notes.back: D) Advance the propeller control (rpm), then the throttle
notes.choices:
A) Advance the throttle, then the propeller control
B) Advance the mixture, then the throttle
C) Advance both at once as fast as possible
D) Advance the propeller control (rpm), then the throttle
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the sequence and risks high manifold pressure with low rpm. C: the handbook calls for smooth, slow power changes. B: the rule concerns rpm and manifold pressure.
notes.explanation: When increasing power, rpm is raised before manifold pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: When increasing power, increase the rpm first and then the manifold pressure

notes.front: Levelling off after a climb, a pilot wants to reduce from climb power to cruise power. Which control moves first?
notes.back: D) The throttle, to reduce manifold pressure
notes.choices:
A) The propeller control, to reduce rpm
B) The cowl flaps, fully open
C) The mixture, to full rich
D) The throttle, to reduce manifold pressure
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the sequence and would leave manifold pressure high with low rpm. C and B are not part of the power-reduction sequence.
notes.explanation: When decreasing power, manifold pressure comes down before rpm.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: When decreasing power, decrease the manifold pressure first and then decrease the rpm

notes.front: A pilot leaves the throttle wide open and pulls the propeller control well back to cut noise. Which hazard does the handbook name?
notes.back: B) Damaging detonation
notes.choices:
A) Carburettor icing
B) Damaging detonation
C) Propeller over-speed
D) Vapour lock
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are not linked to this combination in the handbook. C: pulling the propeller back lowers rpm rather than over-speeding.
notes.explanation: Wide-open throttle with low rpm is the high manifold pressure and low rpm combination.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Constant-Speed Propeller Operation"
notes.evidence: A combination of high manifold pressure and low rpm can induce damaging detonation.

notes.front: A turbine could produce more manifold pressure than the engine's maximum allowable. Which component lets some exhaust bypass the turbine to prevent this?
notes.back: A) The waste gate
notes.choices:
A) The waste gate
B) The compressor
C) The intercooler
D) The propeller governor
notes.choicesExplained: B: the compressor supplies pressurised air to the engine. C: no such role is described in the handbook. D: the governor controls blade angle.
notes.explanation: The waste gate diverts exhaust overboard before the turbine, limiting its output.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: In order not to exceed the maximum allowable manifold pressure, a bypass or waste gate is used so that some of the exhaust is diverted overboard before it passes through the turbine.

notes.front: A normalized (altitude-turbocharged) airplane has a critical altitude of 16,000 feet. Climbing through 19,000 feet at full throttle, what should the pilot expect?
notes.back: C) Manifold pressure decreasing as altitude is gained
notes.choices:
A) Manifold pressure held at sea-level value
B) Manifold pressure rising to 45 inches
C) Manifold pressure decreasing as altitude is gained
D) An automatic over-boost
notes.choicesExplained: A: that holds only up to the critical altitude. B: 45 inches belongs to some ground-boosted takeoffs. D: nothing in the handbook links climbing past the critical altitude to over-boost.
notes.explanation: Above the critical altitude the turbocharger cannot keep sea-level manifold pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Above the critical altitude, the manifold pressure decreases as additional altitude is gained.

notes.front: Advancing the throttle normally for takeoff in a turbocharged airplane, the pilot sees manifold pressure shoot past its maximum. What should she do?
notes.back: B) Retard the throttle smoothly to bring manifold pressure below the maximum
notes.choices:
A) Pull the mixture to idle cut-off
B) Retard the throttle smoothly to bring manifold pressure below the maximum
C) Increase rpm to absorb the pressure
D) Continue: over-boost is normal on takeoff
notes.choicesExplained: A would stop the engine. C is not the handbook procedure. D: an excessive rise is an over-boost condition to be corrected.
notes.explanation: The handbook's first action for over-boost is to retard the throttle smoothly.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Over-Boost Condition"
notes.evidence: Immediately retard the throttle smoothly to limit the manifold pressure below the maximum for the rpm and mixture setting.

notes.front: In one airplane, moving the gear switch to the up position starts a motor that drives an actuator screw and torque tube until a limit switch trips. Which kind of retraction system is it?
notes.back: B) Electrical
notes.choices:
A) Hydraulic
B) Electrical
C) Pneumatic
D) Manual
notes.choicesExplained: A: a hydraulic system moves the gear with pressurised fluid. C and D do not describe a motor-driven screw.
notes.explanation: A motor turning shafts, gears and an actuator screw is the electrical system the handbook describes.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Systems"
notes.evidence: When a switch in the flight deck is moved to the UP position, the electric motor operates. Through a system of shafts, gears, adapters, an actuator screw, and a torque tube, a force is transmitted to the drag strut linkages.

notes.front: Descending to the traffic pattern, a pilot reduces power with the gear still up and a horn sounds. What is it most likely telling her?
notes.back: B) The airplane is configured for landing but the gear is not down and locked
notes.choices:
A) The stall is imminent
B) The airplane is configured for landing but the gear is not down and locked
C) The waste gate has failed
D) The flaps are over-speed
notes.choicesExplained: A: this horn is tied to throttle, flap or airspeed settings with the gear retracted, not to the stall. C and D are not what this horn signals.
notes.explanation: Reducing power with the gear retracted is one of the conditions linked to the gear warning horn.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: Normally, the horn is linked to the throttle or flap position and/or the airspeed indicator so that when the airplane is below a certain airspeed, configuration, or power setting with the gear retracted, the warning horn sounds.

notes.front: While parked, a passenger knocks the gear switch to the up position. The gear stays down and a horn may sound. What prevented retraction?
notes.back: D) The squat switch
notes.choices:
A) The ground locks
B) The pressure controller
C) The emergency release handle
D) The squat switch
notes.choicesExplained: A: ground locks prevent collapse but are removed before flight and are not an electrical interlock. C lowers the gear. B belongs to the turbocharger.
notes.explanation: With weight on the strut the squat switch keeps the retraction circuit open.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: if the landing gear switch in the flight deck is placed in the RETRACT position when weight is on the gear, the gear remains extended, and the warning horn may sound as an alert to the unsafe condition.

notes.front: On preflight, a pilot sees red streamers hanging from the main gear legs. What do they most likely mark?
notes.back: A) Installed ground locks
notes.choices:
A) Installed ground locks
B) Squat switches
C) Hydraulic leaks
D) Mechanical downlocks
notes.choicesExplained: B and D are fixed parts of the system, not flagged removable items. C: streamers are not leak markers.
notes.explanation: Ground locks usually carry red streamers so it is plain whether they are still installed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Landing Gear Safety Devices"
notes.evidence: All types of ground locks usually have red streamers permanently attached to them to readily indicate whether or not they are installed.

notes.front: After an electrical failure, the gear will not extend normally. The airplane has an emergency release handle linked to the uplocks. What will operating it do?
notes.back: C) Release the uplocks so the gear free-falls or extends under its own weight
notes.choices:
A) Retract the gear
B) Start the hydraulic pump
C) Release the uplocks so the gear free-falls or extends under its own weight
D) Reset the squat switch
notes.choicesExplained: A is the opposite of its purpose. B: the handle works mechanically, without the failed power system. D: the squat switch does not control extension.
notes.explanation: The emergency system exists to lower the gear if the main power system fails.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Emergency Gear Extension Systems"
notes.evidence: When the handle is operated, it releases the uplocks and allows the gear to free fall or extend under their own weight.

notes.front: What makes an airplane complex, and what makes it high-performance?
notes.back: Complex: retractable gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller. High-performance: an engine of more than 200 horsepower.
notes.explanation: One definition rests on equipment, the other on engine power, so an airplane can be either, both or neither.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Introduction"
notes.evidence: A high-performance airplane is defined as an airplane with an engine capable of developing more than 200 horsepower (see 14 CFR part 61, section 61.31(f)(1)). A complex airplane (see 14 CFR part 61, section 61.1) means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller

notes.front: How does ground boosting differ from altitude turbocharging (normalizing)?
notes.back: Normalizing holds sea-level manifold pressure (29–30 inches) up to the critical altitude; ground boosting uses more than 29 inches in flight.
notes.explanation: Normalizing stops at the critical altitude, above which manifold pressure falls; ground boosting goes beyond the 29-inch standard.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Ground Boosting Versus Altitude Turbocharging"
notes.evidence: Above the critical altitude, the manifold pressure decreases as additional altitude is gained. Ground boosting, on the other hand, is an application of turbocharging where more than the standard 29 inches of manifold pressure is used in flight.

notes.front: How does an electrical gear retraction system differ from a hydraulic one?
notes.back: Electrical: a motor drives the gear like a jack. Hydraulic: pressurised fluid from a pump actuates linkages.
notes.explanation: Some airplanes combine the two, and a hydraulic system with an electric pump is called electrohydraulic.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 12 "Transition to Complex Airplanes", "Retractable Landing Gear"
notes.evidence: Retractable landing gear systems may be operated either hydraulically or electrically or may employ a combination of the two systems.
